NEWS 2026-11-19 The Economic Times (Rajasthan family to give up Rs 15 crore textile business to embrace Jain monkhood; 14-year):
Their decision comes three years after their eldest daughter, Shaili, renounced worldly life in 2023 and became Sadhvi Darshita. Inspired by her spiritual journey, the rest of the family gradually moved towards embracing Jain monastic life.
How did the family decide to embrace Jain monasticism?
Dilip Bhai, who originally belongs to Jaswantgarh village in Udaipur district, moved to Surat and established a textile business. Starting with a single shop, he gradually expanded his operations to three outlets and installed several machines. The business eventually grew into a venture with an annual turnover of approximately Rs 15 crore.
However, while planning further expansion, he met a Jain acharya. The interaction strengthened his interest in Jainism and prompted him to consider renouncing material possessions and embracing a spiritual life.
His resolve became stronger after his eldest daughter, Shaili, took diksha in 2023. He subsequently began reducing his business activities and decided to follow the path of Jain monasticism. His wife and two younger daughters also expressed their willingness to take diksha.
Daughters give up their respective careers
The family's decision has also led the two younger daughters to leave behind their academic and professional pursuits.
Family undergoes training ahead of diksha ceremony
Before formally entering monastic life, the four family members have been staying with Jain ascetics to understand the discipline and responsibilities associated with the path.
Their preparation involves learning to travel on foot, follow strict dietary practices and observe the daily routines and conduct expected of Jain monks and nuns.
The family is scheduled to formally renounce worldly life during a diksha ceremony in Surat on February 8, 2027.

Dera Ballan caught in AAP-BJP devotee feud over yatra
Nabin likely to attend Samarasta Sankalp event launch from dera
Trouble appears to be brewing at the Dera Sachkhand Ballan in Jalandhar, with rival groups of devotees, owing allegiance to the ruling AAP and the BJP, at loggerheads over who enjoys closer access to dera chief Sant Niranjan Dass and how the institution should be managed.
The flashpoint is the BJP’s proposed Samarasta Sankalp Yatra, scheduled to begin from Jalandhar on November 18 and conclude in Varanasi on December 3. The event is a part of the 650th Guru Ravidas Jayanti celebrations falling on February 20, 2027, close to the Punjab Assembly elections. Besides being Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s parliamentary constituency, Varanasi is also the birthplace of Guru Ravidas, revered by the Ravidassia community that owes allegiance to Dera Ballan.
The yatra is expected to travel across Punjab and key areas in Jammu and Kashmir, Chandigarh, Haryana, Rajasthan and Delhi before culminating in Varanasi. In Punjab, it is proposed to pass through districts with sizeable Dalit population, including Hoshiarpur, Pathankot, Gurdaspur, Amritsar, Ferozepur and Muktsar.
The pro-BJP Ravidassia devotees want the yatra to be flagged off from the dera, with BJP national president Nitin Nabin expected to attend. The party is also planning a large gathering of supporters and community members for the launch.
However, pro-AAP devotees have objected to it, calling it “politicisation” of the
dera. They allege that Sant Niranjan Dass is not being allowed to meet the sangat. Social media posts against dera trustees Hardev Heer and Babbu have also surfaced wherein they have been accused of wielding “extraordinary” authority.
The dissenting group wants the launch shifted to Guru Ravidas Dham at Buta Mandi or some other venue.
Punjab BJP SC Morcha president and former MLA Sheetal Angural told The Tribune, “We are only trying to keep the starting point near Ballan. We are not starting it from the Dera itself. We are inviting the entire Sant Samaj to the launch. We may shift the launch venue to near Shri Khuralgarh Sahib, the meditation site of Guru Ravidas.”
On Tuesday, lawyers LM Gulati and Sonia Tanwar raised concerns, alleging that Hardev Heer and Babbu were attempting to take control of the dera’s financial affairs and keeping the dera chief in the dark on key matters.
“The dera chief, being 85, is not keeping well and they have plans to take over the reins from him. The sangat, especially from Haryana, is not allowed to meet the dera head,” Tanwar alleged.
The allegations were rejected as baseless by Satpal Virdi, former general secretary of the Dera Ballan Trust. “Sant Niranjan Dass is fit and continues to meet the sangat regularly. Draupadi (Sanskrit: द्रौपदी, romanized: draupadī, lit. 'Daughter of Drupada'), also referred to as Krishnā, Panchali and Yajnaseni, is one of the central characters of the ancient Sanskrit epic, the Mahabharata (c. 400 BCE – 400 CE). She is the princess of the Panchala Kingdom, described being born fully grown from a yajna (fire sacrifice) conducted by King Drupada. Sanctioned by divine prophecy and narratives of her previous lives, she becomes the common wife of the five Pandava brothers—Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva—in a polyandrous marriage. Attested as a partial incarnation of the goddess Shri, Draupadi initially serves as the queen of Indraprastha, overseeing the kingdom's finances and treasury. She is also described as a sakhi (close friend) of the god Krishna.[1]
The most notable episode featuring Draupadi takes place during the game of dice at the Kuru court. In this game, Yudhishthira, having lost Indraprastha and his freedom, wagers and loses Draupadi to his cousin Duryodhana—the leader of the Kauravas. She is forcibly dragged into the royal assembly and deemed a slave. However, she challenges the assembly, questioning the legality of being staked after one of her husbands had already forfeited his own freedom. After she is publicly humiliated by Duryodhana and his ally Karna for being married to five men, the Kaurava prince Dushasana attempts to disrobe her, but her honour is miraculously preserved, as her garment becomes endlessly extended. The Kuru king Dhritarashtra then intervenes and grants Draupadi two boons, resulting in the release of the Pandavas from bondage.
Afterwards, Draupadi accompanies the Pandavas into their thirteen-year exile after they lose their kingdom to the Kauravas. In the final year of exile, Draupadi lives incognito, disguised as a maid to Queen Sudeshna of Matsya. When she is harassed by the Matsya general Kichaka, she successfully persuades Bhima to kill Kichaka.[2] After the exile, when Duryodhana refuses to restore the Pandavas' kingdom, Draupadi strongly supports the call for the Kurukshetra War, recalling the humiliations and assaults she had suffered and demanding punishment for her culprits. Although the Kauravas are slain, the war also leads to the deaths of her father, brothers, and her five sons. These sons—each born to one of the Pandavas—are collectively known by the matronymic Draupadeyas. After the Pandavas' victory, she becomes the empress of the Kuru Kingdom for thirty-six years. In the epic's conclusion, Draupadi joins the Pandavas on their final journey toward heaven, during which she is the first to fall.
Draupadi is a significant figure in Hindu and Indian culture, particularly noted for her beauty, courage, devotion, intelligence, resilience and rhetorical skills. She is also extolled as one of the panchakanya (five virgins), archetypes of female chastity whose names are believed to dispel sin when recited.[3] Mediaeval classical literature, such as the 8th-century play Venisamhara, introduces several new narratives centred on Draupadi, including her vows of untied hair and to wash her hair with Dushasana's blood a

Introduction
As the central female protagonist of the Mahabharata, Draupadi's life is a tapestry of profound suffering, unparalleled dignity, and intense spiritual resilience. Her marriage to the five Pandava brothers—Yudhisthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva—is a pivotal moment in the epic, governed by complex divine interventions and the circumstances of the dice game. This union, while unconventional by modern standards, was woven into the fabric of fate to ensure that the Pandavas possessed the shared strength and shared destiny required to face the eventual Kurukshetra war.
Draupadi's character is defined by her intellect, her fierce sense of justice, and her unwavering devotion to truth. Unlike many other figures of her era, she is not a passive observer of history but an active catalyst for change. Her questions to the elders of the Kuru court during her humiliation in the assembly hall remain some of the most philosophically significant moments in Vedic literature, challenging the very definitions of law, morality, and the duty of a protector. She serves as the conscience of the Pandavas, constantly reminding them of their duty to uphold righteousness even at great personal cost.
Beyond the historical and epic narrative, Draupadi represents the Shakti (divine feminine energy) that is both nurturing and destructive. She is the embodiment of the fire that purifies and the fire that consumes. Her journey from the sacrificial altar to the halls of Indraprastha, and eventually through the hardships of exile and the carnage of war, provides a template for understanding the struggle of the soul against the tides of Adharma. To study Draupadi is to study the intersection of human emotion and divine will, making her a timeless icon for seekers of truth and justice.
Significance
Culturally, Draupadi stands as a symbol of female agency and intellect in ancient Indian thought. She was a woman who demanded answers, who sought justice, and who refused to be silenced by the patriarchal structures of her time. Her interactions with Lord Krishna, her 'Sakha' (divine friend), highlight a unique dimension of Bhakti—a relationship built on mutual respect, profound understanding, and divine protection. This bond illustrates that the Divine is not just a distant ruler but a companion who stands by those who uphold righteousness during their darkest hours.
In a philosophical sense, Draupadi's life is an allegory for the 'Jiva' (individual soul) navigating the 'Samsara' (world of illusion and suffering). The many betrayals and hardships she faces represent the obstacles that the soul encounters on its path to realization. Her ability to maintain her dignity amidst the most dehumanizing circumstances serves as a spiritual lesson in detachment and the preservation of the inner self against external chaos. Her life teaches that while one cannot control the circumstances of fate, one can control their response to it, thereby maintaining their spiritual integrity.

SOURCE hinduismfacts.org (Draupadi - A Cursed Goddess - Hinduism Facts):
Draupadi, also known as Panchali, was a goddess in the Mahabharata who indirectly helped Lord Krishna establish dharma. She was the daughter of King Drupada and the shared wife of five Pandavas. She was one of the most beautiful women in the Mahabharata and one of the five virgins (Panchakanya). Although her worship is uncommon, she is worshipped as a goddess chiefly in Southern India.
Meaning of the Name Draupadi:
The word Draupadi originated from Drupada, which was her father’s name. The name Draupadi means “the daughter of Drupada”.
Other Names of Draupadi:
1. Panchali.
2. Krishna.
3. Yadnyaseni.
4. Drupadkanya.
Draupadi’s Previous Birth:
There are many different stories about Draupadi’s previous life. In the Vyasa Mahabharata, there is a story about her last birth, which Sage Vyasa narrated to the Pandavas before they met her.
1. Once upon a time, an illustrious sage had a beautiful daughter. As a consequence of her acts (in a past life), she became unfortunate. Though chaste and beautiful, she could not obtain a husband. Therefore, she began to practice ascetic penances to obtain a husband. She soon gratified Lord Shiva with her severe asceticism. He said, “Ask the boon you desire the most!”
Desirous of benefiting herself, she repeatedly said to the supreme lord, “O Lord, give me a husband endued with every accomplishment.” Then Lord Shiva replied to her, “O blessed one, you shall have five husbands from among the Bharata princes.” Thus told, she told Lord Shiva, “O Lord, I desire to have only one husband through thy grace.” The god then addressed her again and said these excellent words, “O girl, you said full five times, ‘Give me (a) husband.‘ You shall, therefore, have five husbands in another life!’
2. According to folklore, Panchali was a princess in her previous life and went into the forest for sports with her friends. There she saw a woman with five husbands. She found it weird and laughed at her. Therefore, the woman cursed her to have five husbands in her next birth.
3. Per another version of the Mahabharata, her name was Nalayani, and she was the wife of Sage Maudgalya. She was very devoted to him. Hence, he asked her to ask for a boon. She asked him to take five different forms and have sex with her. The sage granted her wish and did so. This sport continued for many years, but Nalayania was unsatisfied and wanted more. Therefore, the sage cursed her to have five husbands in her next life.
Draupadi was not born from a woman’s womb; she was ayonija. Both she and her brother Dhrishtyadumna were born from the sacrificial fire.
Background:
Although Dronacharya was a Brahmin, he possessed many divine weapons and was ardent in the art of war. He and the king Drupada were childhood friends. Therefore, he approached him, hoping that his friend would help him through his poverty, but Drupada refused to recognize him and humiliated him in front of the court. Therefore, Dronacharya pledged to avenge his insult.
After completing the training of Pandavas and Kauravas, he asked them to defeat Drupada as his fee for training them. Although the Kauravas failed to defeat Drupada, the Pandavas managed to do so. After insulting him, he took half of Drupada’s kingdom and gave him the remaining kingdom.
Drupada wanted to avenge his defeat, but no one in the world could defeat Dronacharya. Therefore, he decided to perform a yajna and give birth to a son to kill Dronacharya and avenge his defeat.
